To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the loss of cp-ndhs in some orchids is not due to gene transfer to the nucleus, but due to a loss of the ND complex in these orchids, and that the loss of the chloroplast-encoded ndh genes in these orchids is not unique, but is found in many other plants as well.
the loss of the NAD(P) H dehydrogenase‐like (NDH)‐complex‐related genes within the plastid and the nuclear genomes is a frequent occurrence in plants.
the NDH complex, a ubiquitous photosynthetic protein complex in most land plants, can be completely lost, resulting in a photoautotroph to heterotroph transition.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolutionary dynamics of the chloroplast genome, and the evolutionary transition of the NDH-related genes from the chloroplast to the nuclear genome.
the evolution of the NDH‐related genes in the plastid and nuclear genomes of orchids and other plants.
the loss of the chloroplast-encoded ndh genes and the nucleus-encoded NDH genes, and the loss of the NADH dehydrogenases-like (NDH)-related complex in orchids and some other plants.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the NDH complexes are not necessary for all photoautotrophic species, and that the NDH gene family is a good example for gene loss during the transition from autotrophic to heterotrophic life histories.
the NDH‐complex is not a universal component of photosynthesis.
the loss of the cp-ndh gene family and the loss of the nuclear-encoded NDH complex subunits may have occurred independently in some orchids.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the NDH complexes are not essential for the photosynthesis of some plants, and that the loss of the complex may increase the chance for the transition from a photo-autotrophic to a non-photoautotrophic life history.

some photoautotrophic orchids have evolved into a heterotrophic mode of nutrition and that this evolution may have been accompanied by the loss of the plastid-encoded cpndh genes and the nuclear-encoded ndh genes.
the NDH complexes in some orchids are not essential for plant growth and survival, and the NDH complex has been lost independently in several photoautotrophic and heterotrophic plant species.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the loss of cp-ndhs is not the only reason for the absence of the functional NDH complex in orchids and other plants.

the NDH complexes are not essential for photosynthesis in some photoautotrophic species and the loss of this complex may have been an important step in the transition from photoautotrophic life to heterotrophic life in plants.
the NDH‐complex is not essential in some orchids and that the NDH-complex can be lost in some photoautotrophic species.
